text: Two hands-on exercises: computing qubit counts at distances not already tabulated, and reasoning through which stabilizers detect a specific error on the smallest practical lattice.

Using the verified formulas, computed directly for two new distances: at d=13, 169 data qubits and 168 ancilla for 337 total; at d=17, 289 data and 288 ancilla for 577 total. Notice the jump from d=13 to d=17, 240 additional qubits, is much larger than the jump from d=3 to d=7 earlier, only 80 additional qubits — consistent with quadratic growth, where each fixed step up in distance costs more additional qubits the larger the starting distance already is.

Take the smallest practical surface code, distance 3: 9 data qubits, 8 ancillas. Suppose a single boundary data qubit, touched by exactly 2 of the 8 stabilizers, suffers an X error. Following the same anticommutation logic from Chapter 4: an X error anticommutes with Z-type stabilizers and commutes with X-type ones. If this qubit happens to be touched by exactly one Z-type stabilizer, a common situation at the lattice edge, the result is exactly one defect — a single flipped Z-type stabilizer outcome, with every other stabilizer reading normally.

A single, isolated defect is the easiest case for a decoder: it pairs that one defect with the nearest lattice boundary and applies the corresponding correction, done. The harder cases — multiple defects appearing across several rounds, requiring minimum-weight perfect matching's full graph-matching machinery — are what real decoding hardware has to handle continuously once a computation runs long enough for several errors to accumulate between corrections.
Next, Chapter 6 turns everything built so far into real resource-estimation numbers: what a logical qubit actually costs in physical qubits.
